diagnosis.title: Overbroad verification instructions
diagnosis.summary: Instructions make the agent check more than the user’s task needs, often because several files repeat or contradict one another.

definition.p: Verification instructions should reflect what the user wants to learn or deliver, what could go wrong, and how much checking is worthwhile. Rules such as “test after every change” can spread across skills and project files until even a quick prototype triggers a production-scale test process.
The agent may be following those instructions correctly. This diagnosis concerns instructions that are too broad, duplicated, or contradictory; it does not explain every case of excessive checking.

intervention-ref.when: The agent’s active instructions demand checks that do not fit the task, or several instructions keep restarting the same checks.

ul.li: Expected improvement: After consolidating the instructions, similar tasks should spend less time on unwanted checks and reach the user sooner.
Preserve: Checks that the user needs for a release or a credible risk should still happen. The agent should respect when the user plans to do the remaining review.

A reason to reconsider: If excess checking continues under the simplified instructions, examine whether the agent understands the task and application. If defects increase, restore the missing coverage.

criterion.title: The agent is using the instruction
criterion.p: Find the actual instruction that leads to the extra checks, in the loaded skill, project guidance, or workflow. An unused file is not enough.

criterion.title: The instruction asks for too much
criterion.p: Compare the rule with the user’s goal, intended review, and the application’s real failure risks. Explain which demanded checks do not help that work.

criterion.title: Following it creates extra work
criterion.p: The instruction produces excessive verification. Repeated reads may also match repeated retrieval.

exclusion.title: The task needs these checks
exclusion.p: The user wants production readiness, or the proposed change presents a real risk that the check addresses. Extensive checking can be the right amount of work.

exclusion.title: A useful check is slow
exclusion.p: A useful check can be slow because its implementation is inefficient. That calls for improving the check, not necessarily removing its instruction.

alternative.title: The agent has forgotten a previous result

discriminator.p: If a passed result disappeared during compaction, consider compaction loss. The checking rule may already be reasonable.
If the instructions allow a quick prototype but the agent behaves as if it must certify a release, clarify the goal and the user’s review plans.

alternative.title: The agent misunderstands what can fail

discriminator.p: Check the failure the agent says it is testing for. If the application cannot reach that state, improve its understanding of the application rather than adding more testing rules.

investigation.p: Read the instructions actually loaded for one affected task. Mark duplicate demands, contradictions, and checks that do not help the user’s goal; review those findings with the person responsible for the workflow.
